background.definition: Visual impairment (low vision): loss of vision associated with disease, trauma, congenital abnormality, or uncorrected refractive error. The term "blindness" is used erroneously and interchangeably to describe an individual with visual impairment. In the United States, legal blindness is defined by the Social Security Administration as vision in the better seeing eye with correction of 20/200 or worse, or (1) constriction of the peripheral visual field in the better eye to 10 degrees or worse from the point of fixation (2) the widest angle vision in the better eye subtends an angle no greater than 20 degrees.

list.listitem: Data from 2002 suggest that in the United States, 240,000 new cases of visual impairment (low vision) and blindness occur per year. With the aging population, that figure is expected to double over the next 25 years.
Based on data from 2002, an estimated 3.4 million adults in the US have visual impairment or blindness.
Globally, the prevalence of visual impairment in 2002 was approximately 161 million, of whom 37 million were considered blind.
Visual impairment is associated with a loss of approximately 209,000 quality-adjusted life years based on data from the United States.
Globally, it is estimated that in 1999 approximately 1.5 million children were legally blind. The majority are found in Asia, Africa, and Latin America.
See Differential Diagnosis table.
An estimated 4.2 million U.S. adults have glaucoma (2.6% of those ≥40), with 1.49 million affected by vision-impairing disease; prevalence is highest among Black adults (3.15%).
Cataract, trachoma, and glaucoma account for more than 70% of legal blindness worldwide.

In the United States, causes of legal blindness vary markedly by race. Among Caucasians, the four leading causes of legal blindness in order of prevalence are age related macular degeneration (AMD), cataract, glaucoma, and diabetic retinopathy.
Among African Americans, the leading causes of blindness in order of prevalence are cataract, glaucoma, diabetic retinopathy, and AMD.
Among hispanics, glaucoma has been identified as the leading cause of blindness followed equally by cataract, diabetic retinopathy, and AMD.

In a large retrospective study of over 37 million adults with type 2 diabetes, semaglutide use was associated with a modestly increased risk of nonarteritic anterior ischemic optic neuropathy (NAION) (IRR 1.32, 95% CI 1.14–1.54), with one comparator analysis showing a higher risk versus empagliflozin (HR 2.27, 95% CI 1.16–4.46), though most comparisons were not statistically significant.
A comprehensive eye examination is recommended at regular intervals for early detection of eye disease based on expert opinion. Clinical trials have not found benefit in healthy elderly, though. C
The recommended frequency of evaluation is shown in and the content of the examination in . C
Encourage patients in hazardous occupations to wear appropriate safety eye wear. Sinks to rinse eyes following chemical exposure should be available in the workplace. C

There is insufficient evidence to demonstrate benefit of preventing blindness by supplementing with Vitamin A in children with measles, with no randomized trials. A Cochrane review concluded vitamin A use in children with measles should be encouraged for its other proven clinical benefits, especially in low resource countries where diets may be deficient in vitamin A. C
The USPSTF concludes that there is insufficient evidence to determine the balance of benefits and harms of screening for primary open angle glaucoma. C

list.listitem: See Differential Diagnosis table for typical presentation of different causes of low vision and blindness.
Patients with a complaint of visual loss should have be referred for a comprehensive eye evaluation ().
Suspect temporal arteritis in patients with fluctuating vision and a history of either headache, diplopia, scalp tenderness, and/or prominent temporal arteries.
In patients with acute vision loss in one or both eyes also consider narrow angle glaucoma or central retinal artery or vein occlusion.

For detection of visual field deficits, describing the face and finger counting is best at ruling in (LR+ 43), while static finger wiggle + kinetic 5 mm red target are best at ruling out when normal (LR- 0.2).
If temporal arteritis is suspected, order sed rate, CRP, and temporal artery biopsy. Initiation of steroids should not await biopsy results.
In patients with fluctuating vision in both eyes that is suspected to be due to diabetic retinopathy, order fasting blood glucose and inspect fundus for presence of blood or exudate.

In patients with acute loss of vision in one or both eyes or acute loss of vision centrally, measure visual acuity and refer urgently for evaluation by an ophthalmologist. If related to central retinal artery occlusion or branch or central retinal vein occlusion, evaluate for cardiovascular disease including carotid ultrasound and cardiac echocardiography.
American College of Radiology (ACR) guidelines recommend MRI of the brain and orbit (with and without contrast) for the child with visual loss.

ACR guidelines recommend MRI of the brain and orbit (with and without contrast) as the preferred study for the adult with sudden onset of painless or painful visual loss; proptosis and/or visual loss; scleritis, uveitis and visual loss; and head injury with visual loss. CT of brain and orbit with and without contrast is an alternative if MRI is not available.
See for a suggested approach to the adult with visual loss.
See and for a suggested approach to the child with monocular or binocular visual loss.

Associated with hearing loss, poor night vision, color vision deficiency, or family history of inherited retinal disease?
History of headache and evidence of papilledema.
Suspect uncorrected or undercorrected refractive error or malingering.
Suspect brain tumor and/or congenital CNS malformation, hydrocephalus or pseudo tumor cerebri. Obtain brain imaging and ophthalmologic consult.
Suspect hereditary retinal disease.
History of trauma, head injury or evidence of child abuse?
Suspect cortical injury, bilateral vitreal hemorrhage, or bilateral retinal injury. Obtain brain imaging, ophthalmologic consult, and possibly child protective services.

Rule out disseminated encephalomyelitis secondary to infectious or inflammatory disease process. Obtain infectious disease and ophthalmologic consult.
Bilateral disc edema present?
Associated with bilateral perilimbal injection and eye pain not related to eye movement?
Perform physical examination with CBC and comprehensive metabolic panel; rule out diabetes mellitus; obtain eye consult.
Probable anterior uveitis. Rule out probable autoimmune disease based on signs and symptoms; obtain eye consult.

Assessment of visual acuity
Assessment of pupillary and extraocular muscle function
Visual fields by confrontation
Slit lamp examination
Measurement of intraocular pressure
Examination of the fundus
